idiom_name: two-constructor sum type (Ok/Err or Left/Right) with fold/match and map/flatMap
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define one type with exactly two constructors - a success carrying the value and a failure carrying the reason - and let those constructors be the only way to create it. Provide one eliminator (fold/match/switch) that takes a handler per branch so that handling both cases happens in exactly one place, and provide map/flatMap so that a sequence of fallible steps composes and short-circuits at the first failure instead of nesting conditionals. Keep the reason a domain value rather than a formatted string, and convert exceptions into values at the boundary where the local error semantics are known. Unwrap-style accessors (unwrap, get, value!) are escape hatches for tests and documented invariants, never for the production path.
code_sketch:
type Outcome = Ok(value) | Err(reason)

f() -> Outcome:
    x = fallible_step_1()
    if x is Err: return x              # short-circuit, reason preserved
    return fallible_step_2(transform(x))

match f():
    Ok(v)  -> use(v)
    Err(r) -> handle(r)                # both branches are mandatory right here
pitfalls: Returning a formatted message instead of a domain reason makes branching impossible and turns the failure branch into log decoration.
Bypassing the constructors (a nil-means-failure path, or an exception thrown from the same API) leaves two error channels that every caller must handle.
A sum type that stuffs three or more outcomes into the error branch is a general variant, not an Either: the two-case contract is what keeps the type total.
Using map where flatMap is needed produces nested Either<E, Either<E, T>> (or Result<Result<...>>); callers must flatten or the type spirals into unreadability.
Designing error types as unstructured strings (Either<String, T>) makes exhaustive pattern matching impossible and silently invites callers to parse the message text for decision logic.
Conflating network/transport exceptions with domain failures in the same error type forces callers to decode both concerns at every call site; translate at the boundary instead.
Propagating raw exception objects as reasons without wrapping them in a domain error type leaks implementation detail (the call stack, the JVM class name) into what should be an API contract.
Using unwrap/expect/getOrThrow in production code paths outside of tests turns every unexpected failure into an unchecked crash — the Either is then just an exception with extra steps.
Building a pipeline that calls map on a step returning Either instead of flatMap/bind, producing a type like Either<E, Either<E, T>>, and forgetting to flatten at the end.

Forgetting that flatMap short-circuits on Left/Err/Failure: any side effects (logging, metrics, cleanup) placed in the success handler of an intermediate step after a failure are silently skipped — design for total operations or use a tee/tap combinator.

Wrong move: wrapping every failure, including unrecoverable ones, in Either -> the value carries no stack, no cause chain, and every caller is forced to branch on failures nobody can act on -> keep Left/Err for expected domain failures and let broken invariants throw or panic.

Wrong move: assuming Either makes the failure surface self-describing -> the signature says 'can fail' but not how, so each layer adds map_left conversions and wrapper enums to name what could go wrong -> define one closed domain error type whose enumeration is the contract.

Wrong move: adding a Result wrapper hoping it will change failure policy -> the retry, rollback and continuation decisions stay identical and only verbosity and tribal knowledge are added -> decide the policy where the failure occurs and encode it as a value only when the caller genuinely branches.
